item.title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies at 65, bandmates pay emotional tribute
item.description: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor, whose playing powered 1980s hits including "Rio" and "Hungry Like the Wolf," has died at 65 of prostate cancer, his family said.
item.content:encoded:
Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor has died at age 65 of prostate cancer, Fox News Digital confirmed.

Taylor died peacefully at home surrounded by family on Monday, according to a joint statement from his family and former bandmates.

"To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather," his wife, Tracey, said on behalf of the family.

In a tribute on the band's website, lead singer Simon Le Bon wrote, "There’s a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart."

item.title: Pat Freiermuth sidesteps Aaron Rodgers' claims about Mike McCarthy and Steelers coaching staff
item.description: Aaron Rodgers claimed Mike McCarthy dozes off in meetings, leaving Steelers tight end Pat Freiermuth dodging questions as Pittsburgh braces for Denver.
item.content:encoded:
If the Pittsburgh Steelers thought they'd get a relaxing Wednesday before Thanksgiving, they were mistaken.

Because now-former signal caller Aaron Rodgers went scorched earth on Steelers coach Mike McCarthy during an appearance on "The Pat McAfee Show," even claiming that the coach has been known to doze off in meetings.

Now, players like tight end Pat Freiermuth found themselves in front of microphones just minutes after Rodgers' bombshell interview and in a brutal spot.

AARON RODGERS NOT RETURNING TO STEELERS, SAYS MIKE MCCARTHY FALLS ASLEEP IN MEETINGS AND IS 'UNWELL'

"Yeah, listen: anything I say about the situation is going to be tough, and obviously (the situation) is tough," Freiermuth said. "Y'know, I'm here, and we're just focused on trying to get a win against Denver."

The former Penn State Nittany Lion was then asked if he had confidence in the Steelers coaching staff and the team's current direction.

WHAT’S YOUR TAKE: WILL AARON RODGERS PLAY ANOTHER SNAP THIS SEASON?

"I'm confident," he said.

Freiermuth was especially in a bind, as Rodgers claimed that the tight end was the one who broke the news that he was being benched in the first place. He was asked about the conversation he had with Rodgers over the phone.

"I was just checking in on a close friend, from what I heard," Freiermuth said. "That's all I have to say about that."

Freiermuth also steered clear of a question about whether the situation between Rodgers and the organization could've ended differently.

"Again, I'm sorry, but I'm just going to focus on Denver," he said.

It's a wise choice to put as much focus on the Broncos as possible. With the Steelers already facing a Black Friday meeting with the top team in the conference, the last thing they need is some noise creating distractions.

And, boy, is there a lot of drama here, and likely more to come.

item.title: Trump's birthright citizenship restrictions struck down again by DC federal judge he called 'hater'
item.description: Judge Christopher Cooper struck down Trump's second birthright citizenship order, citing the Fourteenth Amendment and rejecting surrogacy-based exclusions.
item.content:encoded:
A DC federal judge, previously dubbed by President Donald Trump as an "anti- Trump Hater," blocked Trump's second attempt to restrict birthright citizenship in a Wednesday ruling.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, who was recently in Trump's crosshairs after ruling against efforts to shut down the Kennedy Center for renovations and add Trump's name to the cultural institution, issued a 67-page ruling striking down an August executive order that barred U.S. -born children whose parents are suspected terrorists or gang members, or children born through surrogacy to foreign parents, from citizenship eligibility.

Cooper's ruling comes months after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's initial executive order, signed on his first day back in office. The order attempted to deny birthright citizenship to U.S.-born children whose mothers were in the country illegally or temporarily and whose fathers were neither U.S. citizens nor green card holders.

WHITE HOUSE RIPS ‘ACTIVIST’ BIDEN JUDGE WHO UPENDED TRUMP BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP ORDER

"As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws," Cooper ruled.

Trump's second executive order was already partially blocked on Sept. 2 by U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman in Maryland, whose injunction protected U.S.-born children of mothers who were in the country illegally or temporarily and whose fathers were neither U.S. citizens nor lawful permanent residents.

Cooper's ruling expanded protections beyond that class to include additional children born to certain foreign government and international organization employees, parents deemed "alien enemies" by the administration and foreign parents who used commercial surrogacy services in the U.S.

"The merits in this case are clear-cut. The Supreme Court has twice confirmed that all children born in this country are U.S. citizens, save only for the small handful who are not subject to U.S. law," Cooper wrote.

In addition to the Supreme Court's June ruling in Trump v. Barbara, Cooper referred to the high court's ruling in United States v. Wong Kim Ark, which determined that a man born to Chinese immigrants was a protected U.S. citizen under the 14th Amendment.

SEN ERIC SCHMITT SEEKS TO END BIRTH TOURISM, REVOKE CITIZENSHIP FOR BABIES OF FOREIGN DIPLOMATS

Cooper noted that Wong Kim Ark established narrow exceptions to birthright citizenship, including for children of foreign diplomats, children born aboard foreign public ships and children of enemy forces occupying American territory.

"While the Fourteenth Amendment may theoretically permit new exceptions beyond those listed in Wong Kim Ark, Congress has not authorized any such exceptions," Cooper wrote.

Cooper argued that membership in a terrorist organization alone does not satisfy the historical exception to birthright citizenship for children of enemy forces occupying U.S. territory. He criticized the Trump administration's contention that foreign invaders could occupy American territory without actually holding it as an "outside-the-box understanding" of what constitutes an occupation.

"To recap, a parent’s purported status as an alien enemy, standing alone, cannot strip a U.S.-born child of his right to birthright citizenship," Cooper wrote. "The alien-enemy exception, properly understood, applies only to children born to hostile enemy forces in temporarily occupied U.S. territory."

Cooper also rejected Trump's attempt to deny birthright citizenship to children born through commercial surrogacy arrangements involving foreign parents, finding that the circumstances of their birth do not exempt them from U.S. jurisdiction.

"Indeed, foreign parents choose surrogacy arrangements in the United States precisely to have the child be governed by U.S. law and have the surrogacy process ‘supervised by a court.," Cooper wrote.

TRUMP TO ASK SUPREME COURT TO REHEAR BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP CASE AFTER 'INSANE DECISION'

He noted that, prior to Trump's second executive order, the State Department recognized the citizenship of children born on American soil regardless of whether they were born through surrogacy.

The Trump administration is expected to appeal the decision and request that the executive order be temporarily enforced while the litigation works its way through the courts, a process that could take months.

"This is just another ruling from an activist judge appointed by Obama attempting to thwart President Trump’s commonsense agenda," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "The birthright citizenship executive order is consistent with the holdings and analysis set forth by the Supreme Court."

The Justice Department could seek temporary relief from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit or seek intervention from the Supreme Court. Fox News Digital reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE WITH TIES TO ANTI-TRUMP CONSPIRACY THEORY HIT WITH MISCONDUCT COMPLAINT

In addition to ruling against Trump's Kennedy Center renovation efforts, Cooper ruled that Trump's Department of Government Efficiency must turn over records requested in a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Trump has called Cooper one of the "Radical Left Democrats."

Cooper is also married to Amy Jeffress, who was Biden’s personal lawyer in 2025 and previously did some work for the Jan. 6 committee.

item.title: UConn head coach Geno Auriemma goes scorched earth on his team after loss to South Carolina
item.description: UConn Huskies coach Geno Auriemma says he's having a hard time coaching this team after 18 turnovers and 27% shooting in a loss to South Carolina.
item.content:encoded:
UConn women's basketball coach Geno Auriemma has never been shy about speaking his mind.

The fiery legend recently took his entire sport to task over the rampant NIL paydays being awarded to incoming freshmen, showing that he still won't hesitate to empty the tank and tell it like it is.

Auriemma's sights were turned inward today, though, as he went scorched earth on his own team following their defeat at the hands of the South Carolina Gamecocks.

GENO AURIEMMA, DAWN STALEY SHAKE HANDS AFTER HOSTILE SCRAP LAST SEASON, AS NCAA MAKES HANDSHAKE RULE CHANGE

The loss dropped the Huskies to 4-3 on the season, and in his postgame news conference, an exasperated Auriemma clearly wasn't happy with the results so far.

"I'm having a really hard time coaching this team. You might be able to tell that," Auriemma said at the podium. "I've got to figure it out. But it would be nice if I could get a little help."

DUKE COACH JON SCHEYER SAYS BLUE DEVILS' UPSET LOSS TO MICHIGAN STATE FELT LIKE AN 'OUT-OF-BODY EXPERIENCE'

While all of their losses have come against top-ranked teams, UConn has never lost three games in the month of November, and Auriemma is clearly not handling this skid (or his team's demeanor) very well.

"It's just so out of character for anybody that's watched UConn play for 30-some years," he said. "I don't even recognize it."

IS IT WEIRD FOR A COACH TO NOT TALK TO HIS TEAM AFTER A GAME, OR IS IT EXTREMELY WEIRD?

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Auriemma bemoaned his team's inability to handle any sort of adversity, something his eight championship-winning teams were clearly adept at.

The 18 turnovers certainly didn't help, nor did shooting 27% from the field.

Now, Auriemma is faced with a turnaround that he isn't used to, and although there's plenty of season left, this is uncharted territory for a program that has become accustomed to winning and winning big.

I don't doubt a coach like Auriemma's ability to right the ship, but he's clearly fed up with the current iteration of his team, and it's hard for anyone to blame him.

item.title: 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed: What to know
item.description: For the first time in its history, the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been moved due to weather, shifting to Saturday amid a forecast of high winds.
item.content:encoded:
The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed ahead of a nor'easter in New York City, marking the first time the parade has been moved because of weather.

The parade has been moved from Thursday to Saturday, amid a forecast of strong winds and heavy rain, according to The Associated Press.

"With severe weather expected on Thanksgiving Day, and out of an abundance of caution, in partnership with the City the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will be postponed," Macy's said in a statement.

"Our team is now working through the complex operational logistics required to bring the Parade to life on Saturday, and we will share additional details as they are finalized," the statement continued. "We are incredibly grateful to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who make this extraordinary tradition possible. We can’t wait to celebrate 100 years of Parade magic together on Saturday."

A Thanksgiving storm is expected to hit New York City, as well as the tri-state area, with heavy rain, damaging winds and coastal flooding in some places expected. 

The iconic parade draws thousands of spectators along the 2.5-mile route, which begins in Manhattan's Upper West Side to Herald Square on 34th Street, the site of the Macy's department store. 

An area of low pressure developing off the Southeast coast will push northward into the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast beginning Wednesday night. The storm is expected to intensify through Thanksgiving Day before clearing out on Friday, according to the FOX Forecast Center and the National Weather Service. 

This story is breaking. Please check back for updates.

item.title: Shane Gillis wishes ex-girlfriend 'the best' after tell-all essay accusing him of cheating and 'red flags'
item.description: Comedian Shane Gillis wished ex-girlfriend Grace Brassel "the best" after she published an essay in The Cut alleging cheating and mistreatment during their yearlong romance.
item.content:encoded:
Comedian Shane Gillis’ ex-girlfriend wrote a lengthy piece this week about their yearlong relationship, saying his controversial "Saturday Night Live" joke about women at the gym reflects how he treats women behind closed doors.

In an essay published by The Cut, content creator Grace Brassel wrote that the comedian pressured her into quitting her job, isolated her from friends and family and cheated on her before their split in August 2025.

Speaking to Fox News Digital, Gillis responded to Brassel’s claims, saying, "Grace and I had some good times together. Breakups are tough, and I wish her the best."

'SNL' CAST MEMBER MICHAEL CHE SHRUGS OFF SHANE GILLIS' MONOLOGUE JOKE SAYING, 'THAT'S COMEDY'

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Brassel said she wrote the essay to help other women.

"I wrote this essay to help other women, and for them to know there is a life past it, these kinds of relationships. The beautiful DMs I am receiving mean so much to me. No matter what age you are, this can happen to you, and I always wished someone could have told me sooner. I hope it can help more girls speak out and stand up for themselves," Brassel said.

Brassel referenced Gillis’ recent controversial comments regarding women’s gym attire on "SNL" being that of "whores," writing that she wasn’t the "least bit surprised."

"Until last August, I was in a yearlong relationship with Shane, and his comments didn’t faze me. After our time together, how do I think he feels about women? He doesn’t like them much," Brassel wrote.

The pair began talking in May 2024 after Brassel sent him direct messages on Instagram, and she initially described their whirlwind romance as a "dream." However, she explained that when they eventually moved in together, it was a "nonstop party," which made it difficult for her to keep up her day job as a social media manager.

She claimed Gillis encouraged her to quit, and when they moved to Pennsylvania to shoot his Netflix series "Tires," she felt as though his expectations of her changed.

"I felt like I was turning into a 25-year-old housewife, someone who cooked, cleaned, did the laundry, and waited for her man to come home from a long day at work. I never said I was capable of all that, but it felt like an expectation," Brassel wrote. "When things weren’t exactly to his liking, he would tell me that I wasn’t ‘being good.’ You know, the way you would talk to a dog."

'SATURDAY NIGHT LIVE' STAR WOULD SIT SHANE GILLIS DOWN 'LIKE A LITTLE KID' OVER PROVOCATIVE MONOLOGUE

She added that she ignored many "red flags," claiming he would say something "remarkably cruel" and play it off as a joke, and noted she felt she needed to start dressing more "conservatively."

"I cried every day. I would call my mom in tears, telling her that I didn’t know if I was meant for this life. My six-month free trial of Sweet Shane Gillis had run out, and it was time for me to start paying," she wrote.

Brassel alleged that things came to a head on the Fourth of July, when she said she discovered Gillis’ infidelity after going through his phone and finding explicit messages with another woman that had been going on for months.

"I scrolled and realized they had been sexting for months and had probably had in-person encounters as well. The floor seemed to give way beneath my feet," she recalled.

Brassel admitted she "snapped" when confronting him. She described punching a hole in the bathroom wall and throwing her phone and a chair before the two eventually went through an on-and-off breakup. She claimed they had considered reconciling, but that Gillis said they could never mend things after she began telling others how he treated her.

BROADCAST BIAS: FEMINIST FREAKOUT OVER SHANE GILLIS COMMENT IS THE REAL JOKE

Brassel added that the outrage over Gillis’ recent monologue on "SNL" gave her "some kind of closure."

"He had flown too close to the sun, and people were finally seeing the man I knew. I had spent so long protecting this part of my life, afraid to speak publicly about it, and then he just did it himself. Finally, some initiative," Brassel wrote at the end of the essay.

She also addressed the attention the essay has gotten in a video posted to her 124,000 followers on Instagram, saying she’s been working on the essay for a month and was fully aware of the "discourse" it would cause.

"I'm well aware of the discourse that was going to happen," Brassel said. "And I weighed out my options, and I think that it is a net positive, no matter what. I can handle the heat. I'm in the kitchen, girl. I can handle the heat."

SWIFTIES CLAIM TRAVIS KELCE DID THE UNSPEAKABLE BY LIKING SHANE GILLIS' 'SNL' MONOLOGUE & THEY'RE NOT HAPPY

Gillis addressed the controversy he spurred on "SNL," telling host Joe Rogan earlier this month that he had promised the show’s producers "no controversy."

"Not to defend ‘SNL,’ they don't approve it. I mean, they could shut it down," Gillis said on "The Joe Rogan Experience."

"But you don't write your set and give it to them," he added. "Unless you’re not a comedian. I’m sure non-comics, they write the set for them. They have writers that write the monologue for them."

"The funniest part was... they were like, ‘What’s going on with the monologue?’ And I was like, ‘It’s not great, but I don’t say anything bad.’ The whole time, I was like, ‘Fellas, I’m giving you a solid C-minus of a monologue, but I promise there’s no controversy. I’m calling myself fat for f---ing 10 minutes. That’s it.'"

Gillis drew criticism from entertainment figures, including actor Dan Levy and former "SNL" cast member Ego Nwodim, after joking during his opening monologue last month that women at gyms "just dress like whores now." 

The appearance marked his third time hosting the NBC sketch seies, which briefly hired and then fired him in 2019 as a cast member over a podcast appearance where he made jokes deemed offensive.

Fox News Digital’s Taylor Penley contributed to this report.

item.title: Thanksgiving flights booked after key hour face double the risk of major delay
item.description: Flights after 9 a.m. are twice as likely to be delayed as early departures, Hopper data shows, as storms threaten Northeast hubs this Thanksgiving holiday.
item.content:encoded:
As U.S. airports brace for a brutal Thanksgiving rush, travel analysts are warning passengers about a common scheduling mistake that raises the odds of a disrupted trip: booking a flight after 9 a.m.

"Flights departing after 9 a.m. are generally twice as likely to be delayed as those departing between 5 a.m. and 8 a.m.," according to Hopper data.

The alert lands at an uneasy moment for American flyers, with 69% now ranking delays and cancellations as their top booking concern, according to a Hopper consumer survey.

TSA DETECTS SUSPICIOUS MOVEMENT IN TRAVELER'S SUITCASE DURING SECURITY SCREENING

A storm system bringing heavy rain, wind and thunderstorms has already swept across the Gulf Coast and Southeast and is bearing down on major Mid-Atlantic and Northeast hubs through Thanksgiving Day, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.

Confidence has also been tested by recent technical scares.

Travelers were shaken by the Nov. 13 FAA ground stop sparked by telecommunications instability.

The ground stop halted departures nationwide, resulting in more than 12,400 cancellations, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation and the FAA.

TRAVELERS BUSTED AT AIRPORT WITH OVER 3,000 TARANTULAS HIDDEN AWAY IN THEIR SOCKS

An isolated outage also prompted a brief ground stop at Chicago O'Hare International Airport on Nov. 24, as Fox News Digital previously reported.

Across U.S. domestic flights from 2023 through 2025, just 11% of departures scheduled before 8 a.m. arrived 15 or more minutes late, according to Bureau of Transportation Statistics data analyzed by DelayGuard.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Because commercial jets typically fly multiple legs a day, a storm or runway bottleneck in one hub can affect later routes. Late-arriving aircraft are responsible for 41% of all U.S. delay minutes, an AirDelay analysis noted.

Sunrise departures sidestep that chain reaction. 

"The aircraft has spent the night at the airport, so there is no late inbound flight to wait for," DelayGuard reported. Morning crews are also just beginning their shifts, so earlier snags on the schedule will not hold up boarding, according to DelayGuard.

Passengers whose morning flights are disrupted have far more later departures available to rebook. 

Evening snags leave fewer options, according to AirDelay and CLEAR.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

In addition, travelers willing to brave a 4 a.m. alarm often score lower fares on a 6 a.m. flight than on a 10 a.m. departure, The Points Guy reported.

"Taking a morning flight gives you a greater chance of having a plane and crew ready to go," Gary Leff, a Texas-based travel industry expert and author of the blog "View From The Wing," told Fox News Digital.

"There's an opportunity to address maintenance issues overnight. So [there's] a likelihood of starting the day with an aircraft that's ready," Leff continued.

"Crew have limits in their duty day. They could run out of allowable time with late flights that get delayed," he added. "Early flights mean starting fresh, and you aren't risking your pilots or flight attendants 'timing out.'"

Picking the right day of the week can sway the odds as well.

Tuesday consistently ranks as the most punctual day at major U.S. airports, with fewer than 19% of departures arriving late — followed closely by Wednesday, according to Bureau of Transportation Statistics records reviewed by DelayGuard.

Sunday sits at the bottom, with a quarter of flights running behind schedule, DelayGuard reported.

Leff said delays have a ripple effect.

"Delays stack throughout the day. If you're on the third or fourth flight operated by your crew or aircraft that day, there were several opportunities for them to get delayed during the day," Leff said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

During peak holiday windows, timing can protect a traveler's wallet, too.

Flying home on Sunday can be the costliest option, with round-trip domestic fares averaging $604 compared with roughly $350 for passengers who wait until Monday or Tuesday, according to Hopper's 2026 Holiday Travel Index.

Aviation officials urge passengers to build extra buffer time into their commute, to stay subscribed to airline alerts and to check real-time airport conditions through the FAA's National Airspace System status portal.

"Early flights mean more recovery options," said Leff. "Not only are there more same-day options left on the schedule, but available seats are less likely to have been taken by other passengers that were delayed."

item.title: Rams star Puka Nacua's MCL completely tore off the bone as details emerge from season-ending injury: report
item.description: Los Angeles Rams star wide receiver Puka Nacua's MCL completely tore off the bone when he suffered his season-ending injury, ESPN's Adam Schefter said.
item.content:encoded:
The details have come out on Puka Nacua's season-ending injury, and the details are grotesque.

The Los Angeles Rams star suffered the injury on the final offensive play of the team's 20-13 win over the Washington Commanders in Week 9. The 25-year-old sustained a grade 3 MCL tear, which means the ligament completely tore off the tibia, which is the shinbone, according to ESPN's Adam Schefter.

In addition to the MCL tear, Schefter said that Nacua "had a tear off the posterior oblique portion of the MCL as well."

"So that wouldn’t have healed with the stability that they needed, and, essentially, it would be performance-limiting with a higher chance of earlier degenerative changes," Schefter said on "The Adam Schefter Podcast." "So they had to go in and repair the knee."

Losing Nacua is a massive blow for a 6-4 Rams team that is fighting for a playoff spot. Although Nacua missed two games earlier this season due to injury, he has been incredibly productive when healthy. In seven games, the two-time Pro Bowler has 70 catches for 715 yards and four touchdowns.

Compounding the Rams' problems, they are now without their top two wide receivers, as Davante Adams remains sidelined with a hamstring injury he suffered in Week 6. Rams coach Sean McVay said earlier in November they were targeting a return for the team's matchup against the Green Bay Packers on Wednesday, but he remains on injured reserve and is out.

In six games this season, the six-time Pro Bowler has 30 catches for 480 yards and four touchdowns. Without Nacua and Adams, the Rams are incredibly thin at wide receiver. They hope Konata Mumpfield, Tutu Atwell, CJ Daniels and Xavier Smith can step up in their absence while also leaning on their deep group of tight ends.

However, Nacua is not the only Rams offensive weapon who is out for the season. McVay announced Monday that Ferguson's ankle injury will require season-ending surgery.

Matthew Stafford will try to lead a win without his top offensive weapons when they play the Packers at home Wednesday at 8:00 p.m. ET.

item.title: Maddow says Democrats can abolish Electoral College if they 'swing for the fences'
item.description: Rachel Maddow says abolishing the Electoral College is "doable" if Democrats swing for the fences after they won huge majorities in the 2026 midterms.
item.content:encoded:
MS NOW host Rachel Maddow said during an interview on Saturday that getting rid of the Electoral College was "doable" for Democrats if they "swing for the fences."

MS NOW's Jacob Soboroff asked Maddow about her thoughts on Democrats getting rid of the system, which has received criticism after the last two Republican presidents won their first elections despite losing the national popular vote.

"My whole life, it has been this kind of theoretical, you know, this hypothetical math problem. You know, if ever enough states to speak for 270 electoral votes all got into this agreement, then it would go into effect, and it always just seems so pie in the sky," she said.

GOP WIPEOUT GOES FROM BAD TO WORSE AS DEMS QUIETLY SCORE ANOTHER MAJOR WIN WITH BIG RAMIFICATIONS

Maddow said she felt it was doable for the Democrats after speaking with Ben Wikler, a Democratic advocate for eliminating the Electoral College.

Soboroff and Maddow said that Democrats could use the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement that makes it so a state will award all of their electoral votes to whichever presidential candidate wins the overall national popular vote — regardless of who actually won the vote inside that individual state.

GAVIN NEWSOM EXPRESSES 'OPENNESS' TO PACKING SCOTUS, CALLS ELECTORAL COLLEGE SYSTEM 'PERVERTED'

Eighteen states have signed the compact, in addition to Washington, D.C., which means the compact has 222 electoral votes pledged to it — 48 short of the 270 needed to take effect. However, Democrats now control the governor’s office and both chambers of the state legislatures in the swing states of Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Nevada.

Those legislatures' combined 50 electoral votes would push the compact to 272 and activate it should they vote to sign the compact.

PROGRESSIVES UNVEIL $25 MINIMUM WAGE PUSH TO SOLVE AFFORDABILITY CRISIS DESPITE ECONOMIST INFLATION WARNING

"There are enough Democratic states right now who have a Democratic trifecta — governor and the full legislature — that puts you way over 270 if they all decided to do it, and you don't need very many states to act right now for that to be operative," Maddow said. "It's doable. I mean, raising the minimum wage is doable. Getting rid of the Electoral College is doable, age limits for Supreme Court justices might be doable. I mean, the Democrats have big majorities and if they decide to swing for the fences, they could do a lot right now."

KAMALA HARRIS CALLS TO EXPAND SUPREME COURT, ADD STATES IF DEMS TAKE CONGRESS

Former Vice President and 2024 Democratic nominee Kamala Harris called for major institutional changes in October during an interview, which included "changing" the Electoral College.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"I believe that we need to expand the Supreme Court. We need more justices on the Supreme Court so that we can have a court that actually reinforces the spirit and principles behind the Constitution of the United States," Harris told podcast host Keke Palmer.

"I believe that we should be pushing for what is possible around changing the Electoral College. Right?" she added.

Harris also lost the popular vote in 2024, making her the first Democratic White House candidate to do so in 20 years.

The system allocates 538 electors to the 50 states and Washington, D.C. A majority of 270 is needed to win the presidency. 

Proponents argue, among other benefits, that the Electoral College ensures that all parts of the country play a part in choosing the president, rather than just major population centers.

item.title: Parents of 5-year-old boy killed in Oregon school shooting seek court order against teen gunman's mother
item.description: Parents of 5-year-old Rhoam Summer asked an Oregon court to force the shooter's mother to release shotgun records and preserve his online activity.
item.content:encoded:
The parents of a 5-year-old boy killed in last month's shooting at an Oregon elementary school are asking a judge to compel the teenage gunman's mother to turn over records detailing how she acquired the shotgun used in the attack and to preserve his online activity before potential evidence disappears.

Lillian and Kelik Summer, the parents of kindergartner Rhoam Summer, filed the pre-suit discovery petition Monday in Deschutes County Circuit Court against Shauntai Nickerson, the mother of 16-year-old shooter Griffin J. John II.

The filing comes ahead of a planned wrongful death lawsuit over the Oct. 15 rampage at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, where John fatally shot three children and a teacher inside a special education classroom before being killed by an armed parent. 

Rhoam, who had been in kindergarten for six weeks, is cited in the petition as the youngest person ever killed in a deliberate mass school shooting in the U.S.

HERO DAD WHO TOOK DOWN OREGON SCHOOL SHOOTER IDENTIFIED ALONG WITH TEACHER, STUDENT BOTH KILLED IN ATTACK

Tim Williams, an attorney representing the Summers, told Fox News Digital that law enforcement informed the family it is reviewing "thousands of pages of communication" involving John and "the underbelly of society," which investigators described as "fans of school and mass shootings."

Williams said police also indicated that at least one person who communicated with John has been contacted by investigators and "intimated" that one or more artificial intelligence platforms may have been used in planning the attack.

"Because criminal liability is much more narrowly focused than civil liability, we are concerned that, without such letters, some of the evidence may not have been gathered by law enforcement, and thus will be lost to time and processes," Williams said, explaining the petition seeks to identify potential defendants so preservation notices can be sent immediately.

911 CALL CAPTURES HERO DAD’S BRAVERY BEFORE HE TOOK DOWN OREGON ELEMENTARY SCHOOL GUNMAN

Citing public reports that Nickerson bought a Maverick 88 12-gauge shotgun around her son's birthday in August and gave it to him as a gift, the petition seeks a limited deposition, firearm purchase records, gun-related communications and access to John's social media, gaming and AI accounts.

The filing also notes John had not attended school since Nov. 25, 2025, and lists his estate, Bend-La Pine Schools, the unidentified gun seller and any online platforms or users who assisted him as potential defendants.

Nickerson's attorney, David Glenn, told the Summers' lawyers she will not voluntarily produce the records, according to the filing.

Fox News Digital reached out to Bend-La Pine Schools for comment and did not immediately receive a response.

item.title: Rodeo executive says Americans are hungry for Western culture and the values that come with it
item.description: As Western culture surges in popularity, The Hondo Rodeo Fest founder James Trawick says Americans are hungry for family, tradition and experiences that bring people together.
item.content:encoded:
At a time when Americans seem to disagree on just about everything, James Trawick thinks there's something that can bring them together: cowboys, country music and a good old-fashioned rodeo.

And judging by the success of The Hondo Rodeo Fest, he might be onto something.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

"I think across America and the world people are hungry for authentic Western culture," Trawick, co-founder and CEO of The Hondo, told OutKick in an exclusive interview.

"Politics has been so all over the place, back and forth, back and forth, and we've been at such odds as a nation — and the world, quite frankly. I think people are just hungry for what we're doing."

What they're doing is combining world-class rodeo competition with major country and rock concerts and a celebration of the Western lifestyle. And since launching in Phoenix in 2024, The Hondo has already expanded to New Orleans, with Tampa next on the schedule in February 2027.

But for Trawick, the mission goes well beyond putting on a good show.

"I think we're all more interested in leaning in toward one another than away from one another," he said. "And it takes something like a Hondo to do that."

Of course, Trawick isn't the only one noticing America's renewed fascination with the cowboy lifestyle.

From the massive popularity of "Yellowstone" and its spinoffs to the resurgence of traditional country music, Western culture is enjoying a moment in the mainstream spotlight.

Artists like Cody Johnson, Zach Top and Lainey Wilson have helped bring cowboy hats, fiddle music and Western traditions back to the forefront of country music. And Trawick believes this particular cultural resurgence has staying power.

He pointed to the popularity of the 1980 film "Urban Cowboy," which sparked its own Western fashion craze, but one that was relatively short-lived.

"It was hot for a second, but it was kind of a flash in the pan. It only lasted a few years," he said.

This time, he believes, something different is happening.

"Here we are, whatever this is, six, seven years into when ‘Yellowstone’ hits the scene, and still really bullish on what's going on."

Trawick says the demand is reflected in The Hondo's audience.

According to ticketing data he cited from Ticketmaster and Experian, approximately 68% of the festival's ticket purchases across its events are family-related. And despite currently operating in only a handful of markets, The Hondo has sold tickets to people from all 50 states and 24 countries.

TRACE ADKINS PRAISES PRO FISHING FOR EMBRACING FAITH AND PATRIOTISM: 'THEY'RE NOT AFRAID'

"People are flying in internationally to experience this because, one, I think they're just hungry for a wholesome, family-friendly, exciting show," he said.

"It's something for the adrenaline junkie, and it's something for parents and grandparents to take their kids and grandkids to."

Of course, when something becomes popular, commercialization usually follows. And with that comes the risk of losing the authenticity that made it appealing in the first place.

Trawick is well aware of that danger.

"Of course, there's always a risk, and that is so important," he said when asked how The Hondo plans to preserve its Western roots as the business grows.

"I've had this conversation with every investor that's come in. At the end of the day, we can get as big as we want to, but if we venture from standing for the anthem, praying before we compete, prioritizing the family — if we get away from those core morals and ethics that come along with Western culture, this community, they won't have it. They won't participate."

In other words, he has no intention of abandoning the traditions that define the sport just to make it more palatable to a mainstream audience.

In fact, he sees those traditions as part of the appeal.

"I wholeheartedly believe that if you say 'yes, ma'am' and 'no, ma'am,' and a man holds a door for a lady, and you just take simple measures of respect, though they may be traditional, I think they're good for us," Trawick said.

He continued: "There's respect and dignity in this community like no other community I've ever experienced. This is one that I grew up in, and I just feel like if we can carry a little bit of that out into the world, we can see some healing and some unity."

And that's precisely what he hopes to accomplish by bringing Western culture into major American cities.

Trawick knows the rodeo world well. He grew up in the sport and competed himself before eventually accepting that a professional career wasn't in the cards.

He went on to spend 15 years working in film production, including hunting and fishing projects and content for Western brands.

Eventually, he teamed up with business partner, Blake Cody, a former aspiring musician who had since built a trucking business. Together, they came up with an idea to combine their respective worlds into one massive entertainment event.

The first Hondo Rodeo Fest drew roughly 60,000 to 65,000 attendees in Phoenix in 2024, according to Trawick. The following year, he said, ticket sales approached 100,000.

Part of the appeal is the unusual format.

Each day begins with a free street festival featuring Western vendors, food and live music. In the evening, fans head inside for two hours of elite rodeo competition, followed by two major concerts — all included in a single ticket.

But the concerts aren't just an added attraction. They're also a way to introduce new fans to the sport.

Trawick explained that rodeo is traditionally fragmented across hundreds of sanctioned events, making it difficult for fans to consistently watch the world's best competitors face off. The Hondo instead brings eight of the top contestants in each discipline together to compete for a purse exceeding $1 million.

"If you go to the NFL, you go to the NBA, you get to see the best head to head," he explained. "With the Hondo, you got eight of the world's best going head to head. So every single ride, every single run, you're watching somebody that could win that weekend."

And he's already seeing evidence that the approach is working.

"At our first show, people kind of trickled into the rodeo for the concert. Majority of the reason why they bought the ticket was for the concert," he said. "But when they saw our version of rodeo, they came earlier. You saw it happen across the weekend, just in three days."

Trawick also wants the athletes themselves to benefit from that exposure.

The Hondo works to help competitors secure media appearances and endorsement opportunities. It even reserves premium concert seating for them, treating the cowboys and cowgirls like the professional sports stars they are.

"We carve out part of our floor, our pit, right in front of the stage, just for them," he said. "So it's the most expensive inventory that we have to sell. It's set aside just for them, prioritizing them as the stars that they are."

Following its latest Phoenix event in November, The Hondo is preparing to bring its rodeo-and-music spectacle to Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Fla., from Feb. 26-28.

The lineup includes Cody Johnson, Jason Aldean, Nickelback, Jon Pardi, The Red Clay Strays and Dexter and The Moonrocks.

The festival will then return to New Orleans in April and Phoenix in November, with discussions underway about additional markets in 2028 and 2029.

But as Trawick looks toward the future, he believes the experience of gathering people together in person is just as important as the entertainment itself.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

"You cannot trade digital for a lived experience in any context," he said. "What you'll feel, what you'll see, the people that you'll meet, all of my words will come to life."

And in a country where finding common ground can feel increasingly difficult, Trawick is betting there's still plenty to be found in a rodeo arena.

item.title: Aaron Rodgers gets absolutely humiliated, Curt Cignetti is fuming & Chiefs Heiress Gracie Hunt works in a lift
item.description: Aaron Rodgers was benched for Mason Rudolph on Thanksgiving Eve, and reports say he skipped the Steelers facility as questions swirl behind the scenes.
item.content:encoded:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com.

Final Hump Day of November AND it's Thanksgiving Eve?

Goodness gracious. How lucky are we?

Wait ... there's also an NFL game tonight? On a holiday Wednesday? And it's a good one (on paper)? And we get more football tomorrow, Friday, Saturday, Sunday and Monday?!

Come on. Are we blessed, or what?

Let's roll.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Welcome to a Hump Day Nightcaps — the one where we now live in a world where Aaron Rodgers has been benched for Mason Rudolph. Didn't think I'd ever type that. Still not sure if it's real.

The stupid autocorrect function tried to fix it three times before it finally let it go through. Even the woke AI bot doesn't believe it!

AARON RODGERS AND MIKE MCCARTHY DISAGREEMENTS AT HEART OF QUARTERBACK'S BENCHING BY THE STEELERS

What else? I've got the worst call of the college football season taking place last night in a #MACtion classic, Curt Cignetti went on a reposting SPREE after Indiana was dropped out of the college football playoffs, and Chiefs Heiress Gracie Hunt works in one final pre-Thanksgiving workout before the big day.

This is how you meal prep, boys and girls. Take notes.

OK, grab you an injector and a turkey, and settle in for one final November Hump Day 'Cap!

This is a "put your hard hat on and try to stay under the radar so you can cut out early for the holiday" kind of day, so we're gonna keep this class short(ish) and sweet. We've got things to do and turkeys to prep.

The big story of the day is Aaron Rodgers. Duh. I was STUNNED when I saw it come across my desk last night.

"Aaron Rodgers benched for Mason Rudolph." I couldn't believe it. The first question that came to my mind?

Is this the most humiliating thing that's ever happened to a future first ballot Hall of Famer? I'm serious. Think about it ...

Reports are that Aaron didn't show up to the facility today, which isn't surprising. Obviously, there's been some sort of falling out behind the scenes. You don't bench Aaron Rodgers based on poor play alone. Something is stinky here, and I assume we'll all find out together over the next day or so.

UPDATE: Aaron just went on McAfee and stuffed Mike McCarthy in a locker, which, frankly, is impressive. I've never seen anything like it. 

So, yes … falling out it is! 

Lordy. 

The Steelers, by the way, are a disaster. Rodgers hasn't looked great, but that team is horrible. Look at their remaining schedule. There is maybe one winnable game left. This is about to get nasty.

But that's a story for another day. Right now, we're here to discuss Aaron Rodgers. He's become a lightning rod in recent years, but if you're old enough to remember him in his prime, there wasn't a better thrower of the ball (whatever that means) than Aaron Rodgers.

What an incredible fall from grace:

I remember that playoff game like it was yesterday. One of the best playoff games of my lifetime. Again, nobody spun the rock quite like Aaron back in the day.

Since then, it's been a disaster ...

Two horrendous years with the Jets, followed by 18 disappointing months in Pittsburgh. And now, he's been benched. It HAS to be up there for biggest downfalls ... ever? Can you think of a superstar athlete who's career plummeted worse toward the end?

I can't.

Thoughts from any Steelers fans in class today? Let me know! Zach.Dean@OutKick.com.

OK, let's leave the Aaron Rodgers humiliation ritual and head to something even worse that took place last night while you all were sleeping.

Is this the worst call of the college football season?

I wrote about this monstrosity earlier, so feel free to check that out if you want to really get into the weeds.

To me, it's just a horrible call. You don't make that call in that situation. Listen to that poor ESPN announcer. He's stunned. He's beside himself. He's looking for answers, and there's no ref in the booth to offer an explanation.

The ball does seem to slightly move at first when it hits the receiver's face. It's slight, but it appears to move. He basically caught it with his facemask.

Regardless, he still controls it before getting his first foot down. He then appears to get a second foot down just for good measure, although the back one may have been on the line.

Does he lose control of it when he switches hands after the first foot hits? It looks like there's a slight chance of it, but I don't see it. It's certainly not nearly enough evidence to overturn a walk-off touchdown. He never lost control.

That's three times since the 4 p.m. hour of NFL Sunday that refs have made just horrible calls. It's like we've all of a sudden just forgot what a catch is ... again. Did we ever figure it out? Probably not, but this was as bad a call as I can remember from this season.

And buddy, there have been a TON of bad calls. I say it every week — officiating is at an all-time low right now. It's horrible.

OK, let's rapid-fire this Hump Day class into a big Hump Day night. First up? We got another round of CFP rankings last night, and Indiana dropping out of the top-12 was the big development.

Let's see how head coach Curt Cignetti handled the news:

Nobody on the planet has been saltier over these rankings than Curt Cignetti. He's bashed them every single week, and the latest batch finally sent him over the edge.

Now, I don't think Indiana is very good this year. I've said it all season, and I stand by it. BUT ... dropping the Hoosiers out of the top-12 after a 27-24 road loss to Washington is a bit much, no?

Alabama is everyone's punching bag, right? Personally, I think 'Bama would dog-walk Indiana this year, but the numbers are the numbers, and the numbers say if Alabama's in, Indiana should probably be, too.

See? I'm not completely blinded by the SEC. I can be fair!

OK, that's it for today. This class is off tomorrow, so we'll see everyone bright and early Friday!

Have a good Thanksgiving, everyone. Don't waste a single second tomorrow. Eat too much. Watch too much football. Play with the kids (or grandkids). When you're tired, go play some more. Crack a beer at 10 a.m. And another at 11.

You've earned it.

On the way out, here's Chiefs Heiress Gracie Hunt preparing her body for the big day.

See y'all Friday.

item.title: Trump could avoid Dems' ‘extreme’ amnesty push by signing immigration reform before new Congress
item.description: House Republicans say President Donald Trump could sign the Dignity Act this Congress, but warn delay would bring a bill more like an amnesty bill.
item.content:encoded:
House Republicans are optimistic that President Donald Trump could sign a bipartisan immigration reform bill before Democrats take control of Congress. 

They warn that if the president waits until January it could result in legislation containing more "extreme" language that opens the door for amnesty.

"Yes, it's going to happen under this Congress," Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., told Fox News Digital, pointing to the country's labor shortages and Republicans' declining support among Hispanic voters as reasons to pursue immigration reform. "I think it's a win-win for a country, we get a much-needed workforce while providing some accountability for misbehavior."

Bacon's remarks come after Trump signaled during a recent "60 Minutes" interview that he would be open to immigration reform, potentially creating an opportunity for lawmakers to advance the Dignity Act, a bill introduced by Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., in 2025.

WHITE HOUSE DOUBLES DOWN AFTER TRUMP ANGERS BASE BY FLOATING ILLEGAL ALIEN DEAL WITH DEMS

The legislation, which now has over a dozen Republican co-sponsors, would provide certain undocumented immigrants who meet eligibility requirements with renewable legal status and work authorization, without establishing a direct pathway to citizenship.

However, Bacon warned that delaying the legislation until the 120th Congress, when Democrats will control both chambers, could result in a more expansive immigration package.

"Unfortunately, I think the Dems will make it more like an amnesty bill," Bacon told Fox News Digital. "They'll probably go to another extreme."

Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., added to Fox News Digital that "there is no better solution on the table that will get support from both parties while simultaneously standing in the way of the Democrats' looming amnesty-ridden citizenship-for-all alternative."

"The best way to see the work the administration is doing continue into the next two years while Democrats are in control of both houses is to pass a Republican-led immigration plan before January," Stutzman continued.

GOP INFIGHTING ERUPTS OVER IMMIGRATION BILL THAT WOULD SHIELD MILLIONS FROM DEPORTATION

Salazar previously told Fox News Digital that Trump's willingness to discuss immigration reform could create an opportunity to advance her legislation before Republicans lose control of Congress.

"I think that this is a very good window to concentrate on something that even the president said that he was willing to work with the Dems, which is immigration," Salazar said.

TRUMP ADMITS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT MAY HAVE BEEN TOO 'TOUGH' IN FIRST INTERVIEW SINCE MIDTERMS

The bill's original sponsor also expressed hope that Trump could make immigration reform a defining part of his presidential legacy, comparing the opportunity to Abraham Lincoln's role in ending slavery.

Senate Democrats., like Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., told Fox News Digital that he would be willing to work with Salazar on pushing for the immigration bill. 

"I'm here to try to bring as many protections as I can to these families." Gallego told Fox News Digital. "Let's get it going, we're willing to work with anybody to try to keep these families together."

The White House did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

item.title: Presidential contender's 'remarkably tone-deaf’ move against Trump triggers parental uproar: 'Unconscionable'
item.description: Illinois Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker faces fierce school choice backlash after opting out of the federal scholarship tax credit. Critics cite politics.
item.content:encoded:
Illinois Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker, widely believed to have presidential aspirations in 2028, is facing pushback from conservative education and school choice advocates over a move to opt out of a Trump federal scholarship tax credit program. Critics say the decision was made based on politics and not student outcomes.

Pritzker announced Tuesday that the state will opt out of the Trump administration’s Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program, refusing to allow Illinois students to receive scholarships funded through the federal school-choice initiative.

In a press release, Pritzker argued that participating in what he labeled a "school voucher program" would siphon money and attention away from public education while subsidizing donations to private schools that could discriminate based on religion, sexual orientation or other characteristics.

GOV KATHY HOCHUL SIGNS NEW YORK ONTO TRUMP'S SCHOOL CHOICE PROGRAM DESPITE TEACHERS UNION OPPOSITION

"At a time when public school education needs investments more than ever, we should not siphon money from public schools for private education — especially as the Trump Administration’s policies decimate education," Pritzker wrote. 

"We have a responsibility to do right by all of our students. Taxpayer funding should not subsidize donations to private schools that could discriminate based on religion, sexual orientation, or other characteristics."

Prominent conservative education activists and groups lambasted the move on social media, making the case that opting in takes nothing away from public schools and that Pritzker’s refusal simply blocks Illinois students from receiving privately funded scholarships while sending Illinois taxpayers’ charitable dollars to students in neighboring states. 

Many also pointed to abysmal test scores in Illinois and noted that Pritzker is siding with the state's powerful teachers unions.

"It is a remarkably tone-deaf moment from Governor Pritzker, just before Thanksgiving, to deny 1.9 million K-12 students in Illinois access to life-changing educational resources as families are faced with rising costs and an affordability crisis," American Federation for Children CEO Tommy Schultz said in a press release. 

"Make no mistake: The Education Freedom Tax Credit could have unlocked needed resources for families and students, but Governor Pritzker chose to let those resources go to other states."

Schools for America Executive Director Jane McEnaney wrote on X, "Imagine being Governor of Illinois and hating Donald Trump more than you care about the educational opportunities of 1.9 million kids."

PROTECTING FAILING SCHOOLS AND SUPPORTING TEACHERS UNIONS IS NOT A WINNABLE STRATEGY, CEO WARNS

Pritzker's decision comes after three Democratic governors — New York’s Kathy Hochul, Colorado’s Jared Polis and New Mexico’s Michelle Lujan Grisham — agreed to enter the program, saying it brings millions of dollars in additional educational support to students without taking a single cent from public school or state budgets.

The U. S. Department of Education responded to Pritzker’s press release as well, posting on X that by opting out of the program, Pritzker "just handed scholarship dollars from generous Illinois taxpayers to students in other states instead."

Department of Education official Greg Dolan also weighed in on X, saying "the only true thing in this whole statement from @GovPritzker is his name."

"May it live in infamy for so callously and cruelly turning his back on helping students in need," Dolan added.

Erika Sanzi, senior director of communications at Defending Education, told Fox News Digital in an interview that Pritzker’s move was "unconscionable" and a "slap in the face" to parents, who will still be able to write off the taxes. But the money will not go to programs and resources for their children or other students in their state.

"You don't have to like the program, but can you at least describe it honestly and accurately?" Sanzi said about Pritzker’s statement. "They smear it as a voucher program because vouchers is the scary word but, like, putting aside the merits of vouchers, it's not a voucher program.

"You can stay in the school you're in and still take advantage of these services. That's not a voucher program. I wish I could tell you I was surprised by Governor Pritzker. I am not, but I do think it's disappointing. And I certainly have seen outcry from families in the state that are just extremely frustrated not only by his decision, but by what he said in relation to his decision."

Fox News Digital reached out to Pritzker’s office for comment.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

The state's major teachers unions praised Pritzker’s move. Chicago Teachers Union and Illinois Federation of Teachers President Stacy Davis Gates applauded the governor for rejecting what she called "Trump's voucher scheme," arguing that "public dollars belong in public schools" and saying the program would pull money out of public education with "zero oversight."

Illinois Education Association President Karl Goeke similarly thanked Pritzker for rejecting vouchers, calling them a "scam" that sends public money to private schools lacking the same testing standards as public schools.

FIRST ON FOX — The White House accused South Korea of breaking a promise to President Donald Trump to treat U.S. tech companies fairly, telling Fox News Digital that Seoul has since hit Coupang with hundreds of millions of dollars in fines.

South Korean regulators have hit Coupang with roughly $688 million in fines, including a provisional $224 million penalty against its food delivery service, which was announced this month.

A White House official said the administration opposes South Korean President Lee Jae Myung's alleged discrimination against U.S. companies and that the White House expects South Korea to keep its commitment to fair treatment for U.S. technology companies, including Coupang.

EXPLOSIVE HOUSE REPORT REVEALS SECRET OPERATION INSIDE CHINA AT CENTER OF SOUTH KOREA'S FIGHT WITH US COMPANY

A South Korean embassy official punched back at the White House's allegation that there was a direct targeting of Coupang, stating that the nation abides by the agreement with the Trump administration and is committed to a fair and nondiscriminatory business environment.

"All investigations and decisions undertaken by the Korean government, including the recent fine imposed on food delivery service providers for anticompetitive conduct by the Korean Fair Trade Commission have been conducted lawfully and in accordance with applicable laws and regulations," a spokesperson for the Embassy of the Republic of Korea told Fox News Digital. "Furthermore, the right to seek legal remedies under the Korean law is fully guaranteed."

The spokesperson explained that South Korea considers its strategic partnership with the U.S. its most important relationship, describing an alliance built on democracy, the rule of law and open markets, adding that Seoul will keep working closely with American policymakers to correct the record and deepen economic ties between the two countries.

FORMER US AMBASSADOR SAYS SOUTH KOREA PROSECUTED HIM OVER SPEECH MADE ON AMERICAN SOIL

Coupang, dubbed the "Amazon of South Korea" despite having no affiliation with Amazon, is the country's largest e-commerce company, known for its "Rocket Delivery" network that gets most orders to customers' doors the next day or even the same day.

Although nearly all its business is in South Korea, Coupang is an American company. It is incorporated in Delaware, headquartered in Seattle and listed on the New York Stock Exchange.

The company was founded in 2010 by Korean American entrepreneur Bom Kim, who dropped out of Harvard Business School.

FOOD DELIVERY FAVORITE FORCED TO FORK OVER MILLIONS AFTER DOJ ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST AMERICAN WORKERS

A State Department official told Fox News Digital the Korea Fair Trade Commission’s continued "assault" on American companies is threatening the broader potential of the U.S.-South Korea alliance.

The State Department said it is actively evaluating a range of policy options to respond to what it calls discriminatory treatment.

Yoon Suk Yeol, of the People Power Party, was elected president in 2022 but was impeached in December 2024, largely for his attempt to declare martial law.

Lee Jae Myung, of the Democratic Party, lost to Yoon in the 2022 presidential election but was elected president in 2025. The Democratic Party holds a strong majority in South Korea’s National Assembly, giving the party control of both the presidency and the legislature for the first time since 2022.

FORMER SOUTH KOREAN PRESIDENT YOON SUK YEOL SENTENCED TO 30 YEARS OVER NORTH KOREA DRONE FLIGHTS

The Democratic Party is South Korea's main liberal party and favors progressive domestic policies. The country's conservatives have historically favored less engagement with North Korea and stronger ties with the U.S.

Coupang said it has been the largest source of U.S. foreign direct investment in South Korea over the past decade, a claim House Republicans repeated in an April letter to South Korea's ambassador. The company said it drove more than $5 billion in overseas sales of American goods and services in 2025.

WHITE HOUSE EXPOSES ‘TRANSSHIPMENT SCAM’ COSTING US UP TO $26B, POINTS FINGER AT CHINA

"As we have throughout the past year, Coupang continues to seek a constructive resolution that will strengthen the U.S.-Korea alliance, accelerating trade and investment that benefits both countries," Robert Porter, Coupang Inc.'s chief global affairs officer, told Fox News Digital in a statement.

Rep. Darrell Issa, R-Calif., who has been outspoken about South Korea's alleged discrimination against American companies, identified Biung-Ghi Ju, chair of the Korea Fair Trade Commission, as a key figure in the alleged practices.

TRUMP ORDERS MAJOR CUT TO US-SOUTH KOREA DRILLS AS NORTH KOREA RAMPS UP MISSILE TESTS

"For eight decades, America and Korea have benefited from an alliance purchased by sacrifice on the battlefield, joined by economic opportunity, and bolstered by mutual values," Issa told Fox News Digital. "The Lee government has the opportunity to repair or damage our relationship, and I hope he chooses the path of friendship, rather than continued confrontation."

"But that is being put at risk by the anticompetitive policies of KFTC Chairman Ju that have unfairly targeted America’s tech industry and even individual American citizens," he added.

SOUTH KOREAN PRESIDENT JUMPS TO INVEST IN MILITARY AFTER TRUMP CUTS JOINT EXERCISES

In July, the House Judiciary Committee outlined a timeline of the South Korean government's scrutiny of Coupang, from a secret laptop recovery mission in China directed by South Korea's National Intelligence Service to the agency's request that the National Assembly pursue perjury charges against Harold Rogers, interim CEO of Coupang Corp., the company's South Korean subsidiary.

A National Assembly committee filed the complaint, but Seoul police cleared Rogers in September and declined to refer the case to prosecutors. Rogers did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

At the time it was published, South Korea disputed the report, saying that it was based on "unilateral assertions" made by Coupang.

"The Government of the Republic of Korea regrets that the interim staff report published by the U.S. House Judiciary Committee appears to be largely based on the unilateral assertions of Coupang and respectfully disagrees with several characterizations in the report," the embassy said.

She wanted Arizona State to dominate the game from the beginning, "Do not let your opponent dictate the energy, because we dictate the standard."

The forks were all the way up after that. It's plain to see, coach wants to win on and off the court. In order to do that on a consistent basis, there are no nights off.

Coach went on to criticize Arizona State's ball pressure in the first quarter. It was an issue that was corrected after she challenged them.

There's only so much she can do, setting the tone with her style and pregame speeches. It comes down to execution on the court.

So far so good this season for Molly Miller and the Sun Devils. The team has bought in, she's torching the sideline, and they're stacking up wins.

item.title: Doctors warn of lead exposure health risks after controversial Army detonation in Iowa
item.description: The Army detonated five tons of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, and FEMA says residents within 20 miles must shelter until the all clear.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Army blew up about five tons of lead azide, a toxic bomb-making chemical, in a controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Wednesday, raising concerns over airborne heavy-metal exposure.

The mission was reportedly necessary because the substances were "unstable" and liable to explode if tampered with.

While a Trump administration official reported that the detonation exceeded expectations by achieving maximum mitigation, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) warned that residents within 20 miles should continue to shelter in place to avoid inhaling lead dust, and should follow EPA safety guidance "until given the all clear by officials."

IOWA RESIDENTS NEAR AMMUNITION PLANT TOLD TO VACATE BEFORE ARMY DETONATES 5 TONS OF BOMB-MAKING CHEMICALS

"[The] EPA has been on the ground in Iowa BEFORE the controlled detonation, we will be here DURING the detonation, and we will be here for as long as necessary AFTER detonation to ensure communities are safe," the Environmental Protection Agency said prior to the blast.

The agency predicted a brief increase in lead in the air above Middletown, as officials in Iowa and Missouri warned of potential exposure to toxic lead dust.

According to Mayo Clinic, even small amounts of lead can cause serious health problems. Long-term buildup of lead in the body can get stored and slowly re-enter the bloodstream over time.

AGGRESSIVE CANCER TYPE LINKED TO COMMON CHEMICAL EXPOSURE IN NEW STUDY

At very high levels, lead can damage the kidneys and nervous system in both children and adults, leading to complications in the brain, seizures, neuropsychiatric symptoms and unconsciousness.

Children under 6 years old are the most susceptible, as lead poisoning can severely impact development of their bodies and brains.

According to the Iowa Farm Bureau, Iowa leads the nation in producing corn, pigs, eggs, ethanol and biodiesel — commodities that end up in everyday household products." The state also ranks No. 2 in soybean production and cover crops.

One Iowa farmer, Doug Seyb, spoke with PBS about his concern that the detonation could impact his nearby farm, including his cows out at pasture and local ponds that fill the farm's water tank.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The public fears that lead could eventually enter the food supply through crops grown in contaminated soil and livestock raised on contaminated water.

Dr. Stephanie Widmer, New York City emergency medicine physician, medical toxicologist and Fox News medical contributor, confirmed that lead being dispersed into the air is "not a small deal."

"Lead has no beneficial role in human physiology," she said. "In fact, lead in the human body can really mess with biology."

People who eat fresh produce already take in trace amounts of heavy metals like lead, which is widespread in soil — but detonating a "tremendous amount" of the toxic metal raises the risk of dangerous exposure, Widmer warned.

AGGRESSIVE CANCER TYPE LINKED TO COMMON CHEMICAL EXPOSURE IN NEW STUDY

"If there is an enormous amount that is going to be contaminating the food supply, the water, the air that people are breathing in, this is very concerning," she said.

Widmer suggested that Americans near the detonation site should continue to listen to guidance to shelter in place, keep windows closed, and turn on ventilation or air purifying systems.

"We know that lead is dangerous for humans, but we don't know how much, or if any, lead they're being exposed to," she said. "It could be none. It could a ton."

The EPA reported no levels of lead in the air 30 minutes after the detonation, but Widmer noted that just because the blow is over doesn't mean there is no lingering impact.

"Lead inhalation is one of the most efficient ways that lead can be dispersed into the human body," she said, adding that even if it's not inhaled, it can be dispersed into the soil. "It can stay in soil, it could stay in water," the doctor said.

"The very concerning thing is that lead can have negative effects on the human body without even showing any symptoms," she said. "There's still going to have to be testing. Follow-up is really key here."

Among children, lead exposure can cause the following effects.

Besides breathing in the toxic lead dust dispersed through the air, fallen particles contaminating water and soil can also pose a health risk, experts say.

Those who believe they have been exposed to lead, even without showing symptoms, should visit a healthcare provider for a blood test to check for exposure and lead levels, Widmer advised.
